name: The Second-System Effect
statement: The second-system effect holds that the second system an architect designs tends to be the most dangerous system they will ever design.
meaning: Fred Brooks observed that after a first system succeeds despite (or because of) its lean, disciplined design, the architect gains confidence and is tempted to cram every previously deferred feature, refinement, and generalisation into the follow-up. The result is a second system that is bloated and harder to build, understand, and evolve than either the spare first system or a more mature later one.
mechanism: During the first project, a cautious architect keeps scope tightly controlled, deferring nice-to-have ideas. Freed from that caution on the second project, and armed with a backlog of deferred wishes, the architect over-generalises and over-adds, producing excess complexity; Brooks also described over-refining techniques that have become obsolete because the system’s underlying assumptions have shifted.

examples.text: Brooks illustrated the effect with IBM’s move from the simpler 700/7000-series operating systems to the far more ambitious OS/360 for the System/360 family announced in 1964, which he argued contained many instances of misapplied, obsolete refinement.
Brooks characterised a typical first system as "spare and clean" because its designer, still learning, exercises restraint about uncertain generalisations rather than adding untested features.

Brooks recommended countermeasures including experienced architectural leadership, making the cost of added features visible, and disciplined scope control to resist the pull toward an over-engineered second system.

whyItMatters: The concept is widely cited whenever teams plan a "version 2" or full rewrite, as a warning that accumulated feature wishlists and overconfidence commonly produce worse outcomes than incremental, disciplined evolution of the first system.
limits: The effect is an observational pattern drawn from Brooks’s experience managing OS/360, not a proven statistical law; not every second system is over-engineered, and disciplined teams can avoid it through deliberate scope management.
misreadings: It is sometimes misread as claiming any second attempt is doomed, or as being about rewrites of failed systems, when Brooks’s formulation is about a successor to a system that was already succeeding, driven by deferred ambition rather than by fixing failure.
origin: Introduced by Fred Brooks in his 1975 book "The Mythical Man-Month," drawing on his experience leading IBM’s OS/360 project.

sources.text: Second-system effect, Wikipedia. — Brooks’s definition, the 1975 origin, the OS/360 example, and the "spare and clean" versus "most dangerous" contrast.
The Mythical Man-Month, Wikipedia. — the 1975 publication and Brooks’s role managing OS/360.
